context.title: Blueprint SF (formerly TogetherSF) — November 3, 2026 California general election endorsements

subject.title: San Francisco Unified School District Board of Education

positions.statement: SFUSD is in a fragile recovery. Under Kim's leadership as Board President, SFUSD’s [https://www.sfusd.edu/about-sfusd/sfusd-news/press-releases/2025-06-24-sf-board-education-adopts-budget-2025-26-school-year] structural deficit has shrunk and enrollment is [https://sfstandard.com/2025/03/17/sfusd-enrollment-surge-tk/] showing positive signs of recovery . Additionally, he’s [https://www.philkim.org/] well credentialed . He's a former 7th grade science teacher who spent years developing science curriculum. His steady leadership and qualifications have won him the [https://www.philkim.org/endorsements] endorsements of Mayor Daniel Lurie, the SF Democratic Party, SF Parents Action , and others. In the previous June special election, residents [https://www.sfchronicle.com/election/article/sfusd-school-board-22279313.php] overwhelmingly voted to keep Kim on the School Board. Let’s make sure he can keep up the good work and re-elect him this November. Having a steady hand on the Board of Education is critical for SFUSD’s recovery.

subject.title: San Francisco Unified School District Board of Education

positions.statement: Autumn Brown Garibay is an SFUSD parent and PTA leader with a long history of advocating for students and parents. When she was a member of the SF Parents Leadership Council, she was heavily involved in promoting better educational outcomes for students, participating in [https://sfparents.org/sf-kids-cant-wait-press-release/] SF Parents Kids Can’t Wait campaign and raising awareness about unequal academic results using hard data. She has a record of engaging with various stakeholders across the city, bringing people together, and standing up for students and parents in front of the SF Board of Education. She has [https://sfparentaction.org/wp-content/uploads/Autumn-Brown-Garibay-November-2026-Candidate-Questionnaire.pdf] demonstrated extensive knowledge of the challenges facing SFUSD such as the budget crisis, and shown a willingness to take them head on instead of kicking the can down the road. Now she is running for the Board of Education to give families a direct seat at the table. In addition to her advocacy work, Garibay brings private sector acumen to the position, currently working in a senior customer success role involved with strategy. She is [https://www.autumnforschoolboard.com/] endorsed by Mayor Daniel Lurie, the SF Democratic Party, SF Women’s Political Committee, SF Parents Action , and more. Vote for Autumn Brown Garibay to ensure families have a strong voice on the School Board.

subject.title: San Francisco Unified School District Board of Education

positions.statement: While much-needed progress has been made, SFUSD still faces a long-term budget deficit. A financial expert on the Board of Education would help SFUSD right the ship. That’s where Tim Tung comes in. Tung is a finance professional with decades of experience and the credentials to match. A Chartered Financial Analyst (CFA), Tung’s experience includes serving as the Acting Debt Administrator for the City of San Jose for four years and working as a Director for major credit rating firm, S&P Global, for more than decade. Today, he works for a major asset management firm, Allspring Global Investments. In addition to his professional work, Tung has been a member of San Francisco’s Citizens’ General Obligation Bond Oversight Committee, which is responsible for ensuring the City’s bond dollars are responsibly spent, since 2023. Tung’s competence and commitment earned him [https://www.sf.gov/news-mayor-lurie-announces-key-appointments-to-city-commissions-committees-and-boards] Mayor Daniel Lurie’s re-appointment to the committee in 2025. Demonstrating his fellow committee members’ confidence in him, Tung is currently the committee’s Chair. He is [https://www.timtung.com/endorsements] endorsed by Mayor Daniel Lurie, the SF Democratic Party, United Democratic Club, labor unions, and more. Vote for Tim Tung to set SFUSD on the right financial path.

subject.title: San Francisco — Proposition A (Charter Changes Affecting Various City Departments and Commissions)

positions.statement: We recommend voting Yes on A . This is a common-sense measure that streamlines city government. Reforming the commission structure will reduce redundant bureaucracy and create a more efficient and responsive government.

subject.title: San Francisco — Proposition B (Establishing a Municipal Finance Corporation and a Public Bank)

positions.statement: We recommend voting No on B . There's good reason to be skeptical that a public bank would be well-run in SF, especially given that the city's current deficit stems from overspending. Financial experts have also [https://www.sfchronicle.com/sf/article/public-bank-san-francisco-22264570.php] warned that the conditions that make the Bank of North Dakota successful (a state economy that benefited from a fracking boom) don't exist in San Francisco, making the comparison a weak basis for the proposal.

subject.title: San Francisco — Proposition C (Contributions to the Housing Fund)

positions.statement: We are neutral on C. There's no strong case for either supporting or opposing this one. It doesn't add new tax burdens, and the deficit-triggered freeze provision is a reasonably fiscally responsible safeguard. However, this measure doesn’t address the fundamental issue that the cost for building an affordable housing unit in SF is still too high (around $900,000 per some estimates)

subject.title: San Francisco — Proposition D (Changes to Ballot Measure Process)

positions.statement: We recommend voting Yes on D. We support this measure because San Francisco’s current ballot measure system is flawed and results in overly long ballots in which residents are asked to vote on a wide variety of measures that can be quite complex in nature. [https://roseinstitute.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/08/Together-SF-Report_081723_DIGITAL_SINGLE.pdf] 2023’s Rose Report (commissioned by our predecessor organization, TogetherSF) and good government think tank SPUR have both highlighted how San Francisco requires a lower signature threshold for placing measures on the ballot versus other major California cities like San Diego and Los Angeles. These lax requirements lead to numerous problems: elected leaders deflecting from making tough decisions (sometimes on complex topics like taxes) and deferring them to voters, special interest groups placing misleading measures on ballot to support their own interests i.e. June 2026 ‘CEO’ tax, and electeds/groups using measures to wage political battles/confuse voters i.e. dueling measures like Nov 2022 Prop D and E (both related to housing) or Nov 2024 Prop D and E (both related to commission reform)

subject.title: San Francisco — Proposition E (City Administrator's Authority and Changes to City Contracting)

positions.statement: We recommend voting Yes on E. This charter amendment makes critical reforms to our City government’s contracting system. Currently, the City’s contracting process is convoluted and confusing, leading to a lack of competitive bidding and higher costs for the City. For example, the notorious $1.7 million Noe Valley public toilet was a product of SF’s current contracting process. This measure would reform City contracting by giving the independent City Administrator the power to standardize and clarify purchasing rules across City departments while still maintaining important Board of Supervisors oversight. These changes will streamline our contracting process, reducing costs and enhance government efficiency.

subject.title: San Francisco — Proposition F (Changes to Executive Branch Management)

positions.statement: We recommend voting Yes on F. This charter amendment makes much-needed changes to SF’s government structure as recommended both by 2023’s Rose Report (sponsored by our predecessor organization TogetherSF) and by good government think tank SPUR. This charter amendment would clarify lines of authority and thus accountability in government, making it clear that the elected Mayor is responsible for department performance by giving the Mayor direct hire/fire authority over department heads. Additionally, this charter amendment creates a clear system for holding un-elected commissioners by giving their appointing authorities (typically the elected Mayor or elected BOS) the ability to directly remove them. Finally, this measure gives the Mayor the flexibility to merge redundant City departments and agencies + hire deputy Mayors to help manage SF’s sprawling City government. Overall, this measure will create a more effective and accountable City Hall that will be better structured to address resident needs.

subject.title: San Francisco — Proposition G (Allowing Private Vehicles on the Great Highway in Sunset Dunes Park)

positions.statement: We are neutral on G. There are good arguments on both sides here, and reasonable San Franciscans have landed in different places. But the Great Highway has now consumed multiple election cycles. We're taking no position on Prop G and encouraging voters to decide it themselves-then let the city turn its attention to the problems that affect all of us.

subject.title: San Francisco — Proposition H (Parcel Tax to Fund Public Muni Operations)

positions.statement: We recommend voting No on H. Transit is important. But so is everything the city provides -that doesn’t mean we keep charging taxpayers more instead of fixing the city budget. SF residents already pay some of the highest taxes in the country and our city has a high cost of living. When we’re in the middle of a cost of living crisis, the last thing our residents need is a new tax that will heavily impact homeowners and renters. Additionally, this tax measure disappointingly does not require SFMTA to make structural financial changes to help address its financial deficit.

subject.title: San Francisco — Proposition I (Changes to Real Property Transfer Tax)

positions.statement: We recommend voting No on I. This measure moves General Fund money into an earmarked fund, which means the city loses flexibility to use those dollars where they're needed most, like covering budget shortfalls. The city is already facing a General Fund budget deficit. This will only make it worse.

subject.title: San Francisco — Proposition J (Removal of Foreclosure Exemption for Real Property Transfer Tax)

positions.statement: We recommend voting No on J. Originally, this measure was supposed to be paired with a reduction in the real transfer tax to be part of a revenue-neutral package. But now that it’s not, all this measure does is raise taxes, hampering Downtown’s recovery. And by just raising revenue, this measure doesn't address the real cause of SF's deficit: overspending. SF doesn't have a revenue problem. It has a spending problem. Reaching for more revenue avoids tackling that fundamental issue.
